modules.title: NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and the Rubin Roadmap: H100/H200/B200/GB200 NVL72 to Vera Rubin NVL72
modules.description: H100/H200 (Hopper) and B200/GB200 NVL72 (Blackwell) architecture, precision formats, and NVLink scale-up, with the arithmetic behind NVIDIA's own performance claims unpacked, plus the officially-announced Rubin/Vera Rubin roadmap.
modules.scope: In: Hopper SM architecture (H100/H200 fourth-gen tensor cores, FP8 Transformer Engine, HBM3/HBM3e capacity and bandwidth, NVLink4 900GB/s), Blackwell architecture (B200/GB200 dual-die design, second-gen Transformer Engine, native NVFP4, NVLink5/NVSwitch scale-up to the NVL72 domain), GB200 NVL72 rack-scale specs (Grace CPU pairing, 72-GPU NVLink domain, aggregate FLOPS/memory/bandwidth), and the Rubin roadmap now grounded in NVIDIA's own official announcements (Vera CPU + Rubin GPU platform, sixth-gen NVLink, Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, Rubin CPX disaggregated-prefill GPU, and NVIDIA's own '10x lower inference token cost' and '2H 2026' claims) — treated as a real, citable subject, not a bounded unverified aside, but every figure still flagged where it is vendor-projected/pre-shipment rather than independently measured. Out: AMD/Google/AWS chips (pages 2-4) — including AMD's own comparison of MI455X against Rubin, whose adjudication belongs to page 6; MLPerf/InferenceMAX cross-vendor benchmark methodology and results (page 5); cloud pricing and cost-per-token/TCO synthesis (page 6) — this page covers only NVIDIA's own architecture and NVIDIA's own published performance and roadmap claims, with the arithmetic behind the '30x' headline decomposed in full. After reading, the reader can reason about H100 vs H200 vs B200 vs GB200 NVL72 vs Vera Rubin NVL72 SKU choice from architecture alone, decompose any NVIDIA-published multiplier into its per-GPU and per-rack components, and state precisely which Rubin-era figures are shipped-and-measured versus vendor-projected.
topics: Hopper SM: fourth-gen tensor core and the FP8 Transformer Engine's dynamic scaling
HBM3 (H100) vs HBM3e (H200): capacity/bandwidth deltas and what they change for KV-cache-bound decode
H100 SXM vs NVL vs PCIe form factors: TDP, NVLink bandwidth, and memory tradeoffs
Blackwell dual-die package: 208B transistors, 10TB/s die-to-die interconnect, and the reticle-limit motivation
NVFP4 and the second-generation Transformer Engine: native FP4 numerics and the claimed 1.5-2x gain over standard Blackwell
NVLink5/NVSwitch scale-up: 130TB/s within a 72-GPU NVL72 domain vs PCIe/InfiniBand scale-out
GB200 NVL72 rack anatomy: 36 Grace CPUs + 72 Blackwell GPUs, NVLink-C2C, unified memory addressing
Decomposing the '30x' claim: per-GPU throughput gain vs. the 9x GPU-count effect, and how benchmark configuration (TTL/FTL, token counts) shapes the multiplier
The FP4/FP8/FP16 precision ladder and what changes numerically at each step for inference
Vera Rubin platform architecture: Vera CPU (88 Olympus cores), Rubin GPU (50 PFLOPS NVFP4), sixth-gen NVLink at 3.6TB/s/GPU and 260TB/s across the NVL72 rack
Rubin CPX: disaggregated-prefill GPU with 128GB GDDR7 instead of HBM, and the economic logic of splitting prefill/decode hardware
Rubin's claimed 10x inference token-cost reduction and 4x fewer GPUs for MoE training vs. Blackwell — what's vendor-projected vs. shipped, and the 2H 2026 availability window

H100 vs H200 vs B200 vs GB200 spec table: compute, memory, bandwidth, TDP

GB200 NVL72 rack topology: 36 Grace CPUs + 72 Blackwell GPUs in one NVLink domain
Precision-ladder diagram: FP16 -> FP8 -> NVFP4 with peak TFLOPS at each step
Waterfall decomposition of the 30x claim into per-GPU gain x GPU-count

disagreements: What does NVIDIA's '30x inference speedup' for GB200 NVL72 actually measure?

modules.title: AMD Instinct CDNA3/CDNA4/CDNA5: MI300X to MI455X and the Helios Rack
modules.description: MI300X/MI325X (CDNA3) and MI350X/MI355X (CDNA4): XCD chiplet architecture, HBM capacity leadership, Infinity Fabric scale-up, and the ROCm software stack, plus the officially-announced MI400-series (CDNA5) and Helios rack roadmap.
modules.scope: In: CDNA3 XCD/chiplet architecture (MI300X, MI325X — 8 XCDs, shared Infinity Cache, HBM3/HBM3e capacity up to 256GB), CDNA4 architecture changes (MI350X air-cooled vs. MI355X liquid-cooled platform, native MXFP4/MXFP6, LDS/cache changes per independent teardown), Infinity Fabric scale-up topology (7 links/GPU mesh, UBB 2.0 cross-generation compatibility), the ROCm framework support surface (vLLM/SGLang/Triton) as it bears on deployability, and the CDNA5-based MI400 series (MI455X, MI430X) and Helios rack now grounded in AMD's own official product pages and investor-relations press release — architecture, specs (432GB HBM4, 40 PFLOPS FP4, Helios's 72-GPU/2.9-EF-FP4 rack with Zen 6 'Venice' EPYC CPUs and 'Vulcano' NICs), and AMD's own published head-to-head comparison chart against NVIDIA Vera Rubin, presented here as AMD's claim with its stated basis and caveats rather than adjudicated. Out: NVIDIA/Google/AWS chips; the full adjudication of the MI455X-vs-Rubin paper-spec disagreement and of the current-gen AMD-vs-NVIDIA workload-fit disagreement (both page 6); cross-vendor MLPerf/InferenceMAX result tables and the achieved-vs-peak GEMM gap (page 5); cloud pricing (page 6). After reading, the reader can map MI300X/325X/350X/355X to memory-bound serving scenarios by capacity and bandwidth alone, knows exactly what changed physically between CDNA3 and CDNA4, and can state what AMD claims for MI455X/Helios and on what basis, pending independent verification.
topics: XCD chiplet design: 8 XCDs per OAM module, CU count per XCD, shared vs. per-XCD cache
Infinity Cache (256MB) role in the memory hierarchy relative to HBM
MI300X vs. MI325X: HBM3 192GB@5.3TB/s vs. HBM3e 256GB@6TB/s and the single-GPU trillion-parameter framing
CDNA3 to CDNA4 matrix-core changes: per-CU throughput roughly doubling, native MXFP4/MXFP6
MI350X (air-cooled, 1000W) vs. MI355X (liquid-cooled, 1400W): same silicon, different power/cooling envelope
LDS capacity/bandwidth increase (64KB to 160KB) and what it enables for attention kernels
Infinity Fabric scale-up: 7x128GB/s (MI300X/325X) vs. 7x153.6GB/s (MI350X/355X) mesh topology
UBB 2.0 platform compatibility and the MI300X/325X/350X drop-in upgrade path
ROCm software stack maturity: framework/runtime coverage (PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, Triton) vs. the CUDA ecosystem gap

MI400 series (CDNA5): MI455X (432GB HBM4, 40 PFLOPS FP4, 23.3TB/s) and MI430X (FP64 sovereign-AI/HPC part, expected 2027), and the Helios rack (72x MI455X, Zen 6 EPYC 'Venice' CPUs, Pensando 'Vulcano' NICs, 2.9 EF FP4, 2H 2026 volume deployment)
AMD's own MI455X-vs-Vera-Rubin comparison chart: what it claims and why it's AMD's characterization on an unstated basis, not an independently verified head-to-head (full adjudication on page 6)
DRAM-bandwidth-per-FLOP ratio (bytes/FLOP) as the lens for memory- vs. compute-bound regimes across CDNA3/CDNA4/CDNA5
figures: XCD chiplet diagram: 8 dies, CU count, L1/L2/Infinity Cache hierarchy
MI300X/MI325X/MI350X/MI355X spec table: compute units, HBM, bandwidth, TDP

modules.title: Google TPU v5e/v5p/v6e/v7: Pod Architecture from Trillium to Ironwood
modules.description: TensorCore/MXU design, ICI torus topologies, and the pod-scale architecture from TPU v5e/v5p through Trillium (v6e) to Ironwood (v7), Google's first inference-first TPU generation.
modules.scope: In: TensorCore/MXU/SparseCore building blocks, per-chip compute/memory/ICI specs for v5e, v5p, v6e (Trillium), and TPU7x (Ironwood), 2D vs. 3D torus topology and pod sizes (256 to 9,216 chips), Ironwood's dual-chiplet package and its explicit prefill/decode inference-era design intent, and Optical Circuit Switching at superpod scale. Out: NVIDIA/AMD/AWS chips, TPU cost-per-token figures and official TPU on-demand/committed-use pricing (both page 6, including the TPU-cost disagreement now doubly grounded by Google's own pricing page), MLPerf Inference/Training TPU submission history (page 5). After reading, the reader can pick v5e vs. v6e vs. Ironwood by workload (cost-optimized serving vs. training vs. max-scale inference) from chip/pod architecture alone.
topics: TensorCore + MXU count per chip and how peak bf16/int8 TFLOPS is derived from them
v5e vs. v5p split: inference/cost-optimized (v5e) vs. training/performance (v5p) design intent
ICI bandwidth and torus dimensionality: 2D torus (v5e, v6e) vs. 3D torus (v5p)
Pod scale-out limits: v5e 256-chip serving slices (1x1/2x2/2x4) vs. v5p 6144-chip single-slice / 18,432-chip multislice
v6e (Trillium) generational jump: 918 TFLOPs bf16, SparseCore addition, 800GBps ICI
Ironwood dual-chiplet package: two self-contained chiplets with 96GB HBM each, and why this departs from monolithic-die predecessors
Ironwood's inference-era design: large-batch prefill vs. bandwidth-bound decode as explicit codesign targets
Superpod fabric: 3D torus plus Optical Circuit Switching, the 9,216-chip cube-of-cubes topology
Perf/watt trajectory: Ironwood at 2x Trillium and roughly 30x the 2018 first-generation Cloud TPU
Serving-slice constraints (Sax, multi-host inference) as a practical deployment ceiling distinct from peak pod size

Ironwood dual-chiplet package diagram: 2x (TensorCore + 2 SparseCores + 96GB HBM)

Perf/watt bar chart across TPU generations (2018 TPU to Ironwood)

modules.title: AWS Trainium and Inferentia: NeuronCore Architecture and Instance Topology
modules.description: NeuronCore v1-v3 evolution across Inferentia1/2 and Trainium1/2, Trn2 UltraServer/NeuronLink scale-up topology, and the Neuron SDK programmability model.
modules.scope: In: NeuronCore-v1 (Inferentia1) through NeuronCore-v3 (Trainium2) compute/memory specs, Inf1/Inf2 and Trn2 instance-family scaling (chip count, memory, bandwidth per instance size), Trn2 UltraServer topology (64-chip NeuronLink domain), NeuronLink/EFA interconnect bandwidths, and Neuron SDK programmability features (dynamic shapes, stochastic rounding, GPSIMD custom ops). Trainium3 is included only as brief forward-roadmap context. Out: NVIDIA/AMD/Google chips, cross-vendor cost-per-token figures and official AWS instance pricing (page 6), MLPerf Inference/InferenceMAX/MLPerf Training AWS coverage (AWS has zero submissions to any of the three as of this research — a documented, confirmed gap treated in full on page 5, not filled here). After reading, the reader can size an Inf2 or Trn2 deployment by chip count and memory alone, and knows what changed mechanically between Inferentia1->2 and Trainium1->2 (NeuronCore v1->v2->v3).

modules.title: Inference and Training Benchmarking: MLPerf and InferenceMAX Methodology, Batch-Scaling Mechanics
modules.description: How tokens/sec, tokens/sec/user, and cost-per-token are actually measured (MLPerf Inference scenarios, InferenceMAX methodology) and derived, plus MLPerf Training's time-to-train methodology and cross-vendor results as a supporting data point.
modules.scope: In: MLPerf Inference methodology (Offline/Server/Interactive scenarios, closed vs. open division, submission counts and generational deltas across v5.0/v5.1), InferenceMAX's independent open-source-framework methodology (vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM, fixed sequence-length patterns, infinite-request-rate-with-concurrency-cap design) and its headline cross-vendor results, the arithmetic linking batch size/concurrency to tokens/sec vs. tokens/sec/user, why prefill and decode sit in different roofline regimes (compute-bound vs. memory-bandwidth-bound), how vendor-submitted MLPerf Inference numbers can diverge from independent measurements, and — as a supporting data point alongside the inference focus, not a scope change — MLPerf Training's methodology (time-to-train to a fixed accuracy target) and its v5.0/v5.1 cross-vendor results for NVIDIA, AMD, and Google, including the explicitly documented fact that AWS Trainium has never submitted to MLPerf Training in any round. Out: TCO/cost-per-token vendor comparison, cloud pricing, and workload-fit verdicts (page 6); individual chip specs (pages 1-4, referenced not repeated); using training-benchmark results as a substitute for an inference-serving decision — they are presented as a corroborating software-maturity/scaling signal only. After reading, the reader can read any MLPerf Inference, MLPerf Training, or InferenceMAX chart correctly — knowing what scenario, division, framework, or accuracy target produced each number — and can state exactly which vendors have (and have not) submitted to which benchmark suite.
topics: MLPerf Inference scenarios: Offline, Server, Interactive — what each measures and why Interactive was added in v5.0
MLPerf closed vs. open division and what 'achieved' vs. 'peak theoretical' performance means
MLPerf Inference v5.0 vs. v5.1 generational deltas: submission growth, new benchmarks (Llama 3.1 405B, DeepSeek-R1), new accelerators per round
InferenceMAX methodology: fixed input/output token patterns (chat/reasoning/summarization), random sequences to defeat prefix caching, infinite-request-rate with a concurrency cap
The tokens/sec vs. tokens/sec/user tradeoff curve, and tokens/sec-per-provisioned-megawatt as the power-normalized variant
Prefill (compute-bound, large-batch) vs. decode (memory-bandwidth-bound, KV-cache-limited) roofline arithmetic
Multi-token prediction (MTP) as a throughput-interactivity lever: 2-3x gains at iso-interactivity
Where vendor-submitted (TRT-LLM-tuned) MLPerf Inference numbers diverge from open-source-framework (vLLM/SGLang) InferenceMAX numbers, and why

MLPerf Training methodology: time-to-train-to-target-accuracy as the scoring metric vs. inference's tokens/sec — same standards body, different measurement paradigm, same recurring reference benchmarks (Llama 3.1 405B pretraining, Llama 2 70B LoRA, Flux.1, R-GAT, RetinaNet, DLRM-DCNv2)

MLPerf Training v5.0/v5.1 cross-vendor results: NVIDIA Blackwell 2.2-2.6x over Hopper per-benchmark and Blackwell Ultra's further gains, AMD's first-ever submission (MI325X 8% ahead of H200 on Llama 2 70B LoRA, first multi-node Instinct training run), Google Trillium vs. v5p (1.8x perf/$, most recent official comparison still the v4.1 round)
AWS Trainium's complete absence from every MLPerf Training round to date — a confirmed, documented gap, and how to read AWS's own peak-FLOPS training claims in that light
Reading a crossover chart: which hardware wins below vs. above a given tok/s/user interactivity threshold, and why the crossover point itself is the useful artifact, not a single 'winner'

modules.title: Choosing Inference Hardware: Model-Size Fit, Cloud Pricing, and TCO Across Vendors
modules.description: Cross-vendor decision framework mapping 7B-400B+ parameter models to chip/cluster configurations, cost-per-token and official cloud pricing by vendor, and where the TPU-cost, AMD-vs-NVIDIA, and next-gen-roadmap claims fall apart under independent data.
modules.scope: In: model-size-to-hardware fit (single-chip vs. multi-chip vs. multi-node parallelism thresholds by memory capacity: 7B/13B on a single accelerator, 70B needing tensor parallelism or a high-capacity chip, 400B+/1T+ MoE needing rack-scale domains), cost-per-million-tokens comparisons at matched interactivity points, official cloud on-demand/committed-use pricing across AWS/GCP/Azure for every chip family covered on pages 1-4 (a genuine $/hour dimension distinct from and complementary to the $/million-tokens data), the TPU-cost disagreement resolved with two independent lines of evidence (Artificial Analysis measured data and Google's own pricing page), the AMD-vs-NVIDIA disagreement resolved workload-by-workload, a next-gen preview adjudicating the Rubin-vs-MI455X paper-spec disagreement (with the explicit caveat that neither part has shipped or been independently benchmarked), MLPerf Training results treated as a secondary corroborating signal (not a serving-decision input), lock-in/software-maturity/commitment-term axes (CUDA vs. ROCm vs. JAX/XLA vs. Neuron SDK), and a cross-vendor interconnect/scale-up summary table (including next-gen NVLink6/Helios figures). Out: introducing any new chip specs beyond what pages 1-4 established, or new benchmark methodology beyond what page 5 established — this page only synthesizes and adjudicates using facts already established. After reading, the reader can go from 'I have a 70B model, N req/s of traffic, and a $/month budget' to a short list of 2-3 defensible hardware choices with sourced $/token and $/hour numbers for each, and can state with citations where each of the four sourced disagreements in this track currently stands.
topics: Memory-capacity thresholds for single-chip vs. multi-chip serving: where 70B/405B/670B-MoE models cross the single-accelerator line on H100 (80GB)/H200 (141GB)/MI300X (192GB)/MI325X (256GB)/Trainium2 (96GB)
Rack-scale domains as a model-size category of their own: GB200 NVL72 (13.4TB HBM3e), Trn2 UltraServer (6TB), and the forthcoming Vera Rubin NVL72/Helios rack generation
Cost-per-million-tokens at matched tok/s/user: H100 $1.06 vs. MI300X $2.24 vs. TPU v6e $5.13 at 30 tok/s/user, and why this ranking flips in offline/batch mode

Official cloud on-demand and committed-use pricing across vendors: AWS ($/hr for Inf2/P5/P5e/P5en/Trn1/Trn2), GCP ($/chip-hour for TPU v5e/v5p/v6e/Ironwood and $/hr for A2/A3/A4 GPU instances), Azure ($/hr for MI300X via the Retail Prices API) — and how $/hour list price relates to (but isn't the same number as) $/million-tokens

Adjudicating the TPU-cost disagreement with two independent lines of evidence: Artificial Analysis' measured cost-per-token data (workload-dependent, ~5x gap in interactive serving) and Google's own pricing page (Trillium 3-year committed rate of $1.22/chip-hour, more than 3x Introl's unsourced $0.39 claim)
Adjudicating the AMD-vs-NVIDIA disagreement: latency-sensitive low-concurrency (NVIDIA) vs. high-concurrency/large-batch throughput (AMD), with the crossover concurrency points
Peak-theoretical vs. independently-measured achieved throughput gap (14-22% on AMD GEMM) as a general caution when reading any vendor spec sheet, including the vendor-projected next-gen figures below
Software-ecosystem lock-in axis: CUDA/TRT-LLM maturity vs. ROCm vs. JAX/XLA-native TPU vs. Neuron SDK, and what it costs to switch

Next-gen preview: NVIDIA Rubin vs. AMD MI455X on paper — AMD's own comparison chart (40 vs. 35 PFLOPS FP4, 432GB vs. 288GB memory) against NVIDIA's own 50-PFLOPS inference figure, why the two don't reconcile on a stated common basis, and why neither is a measured, shipped-hardware number yet (both ship 2H 2026)

MLPerf Training results (page 5) as a secondary corroborating signal for software-stack maturity and multi-node scaling, not a serving-decision input — and why AWS's absence there compounds its absence from MLPerf Inference

Cross-vendor scale-up interconnect summary: NVLink5 130TB/s (NVL72) vs. NVLink6 260TB/s (Vera Rubin NVL72) vs. Infinity Fabric 153.6GB/s/link (MI355X mesh) vs. ICI 1200GBps (Ironwood) vs. NeuronLink-v3 1024GB/s/chip (Trn2)
A worked decision walk-through per model-size band (7B, 70B, 405B, 670B+ MoE) naming 2-3 defensible hardware choices with the sourced number (including $/hour or $/million-tokens) that justifies each

Cost-per-million-tokens bar chart at 30 tok/s/user: H100 vs. MI300X vs. TPU v6e
